result: Intracameral silicone oil injection creates pupillary block by forming a droplet that seals the pupil, causes angle closure, and can be relieved by pupil dilation. The mechanism involves SO sealing the pupil, aqueous accumulation in the posterior chamber pushing the iris forward to close the angle, and pupil dilation allowing aqueous to flood the anterior chamber and reopen the angle.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 fundamentally challenges the proposed mechanism, stating 'the mechanism of IOP elevation is almost surely not what is illustrated in the figure' and argues that 'the mechanism is simply blockade of the meshwork and uveoscleral outflow directly by the oil.' Reviewer 3 calls it 'silly to assume that the iris is going to bow forward with an anterior chamber full of oil.' The editors also request manometric readings to prove the pupillary block mechanism, indicating uncertainty about the authors' interpretation.

result: IOP measurements show initially lower pressure in SO eyes immediately after anesthesia, then progressive elevation over 12-15 minutes correlating with pupillary dilation, with the increasing IOP closely correlating with pupillary size changes.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 identifies this as 'a huge error,' noting that 'the earlier the IOP is measured after gas anesthesia, the closer the value is to the awake IOP' and questions why the 'totally artificial, pupil-affected anesthetic state' would be representative. Reviewer 3 also points out a logical contradiction: 'if we accept their theory that dilation allowed aqueous to reach the meshwork then IOP should go DOWN at that time point compare to initial anesthesia, not UP.' The editors request reconciliation of how measured IOP is only elevated when pupillary block is relieved.

result: IOP elevation in SO eyes started at 2 days post-injection and remained stable for 8 weeks at approximately 2.5-fold that of control eyes when SO droplet diameter exceeded 1.5 mm, while smaller droplets showed transient IOP elevation.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 questions the consistency and statistical rigor, stating 'these primary data are not only not convincing, the data are not even statistically tested' and notes 'we cannot tell how many eyes are included, nor whether the flags are standard deviations or standard errors.' Reviewer 3 also challenges the claimed consistency, noting that if error bars are standard errors 'there is major variability in IOP...not a consistent elevation as suggested by the authors.' Reviewer 1 requests more detailed IOP measurement methodology and questions whether once-weekly measurements are sufficient.

result: GCC thickness in SOHU eyes progressively decreased to 84%, 65%, 61%, and 53% of control eyes at 1, 3, 5, and 8 weeks post-injection, with statistically significant thinning at 5 and 8 weeks compared to 1 week.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'the manner in which the data is presented for OCT, OKR, and PERG in Figure 2 do not show that there is progression over time' and requests the data 'be presented more clearly.' The editors specifically request that the manuscript 'add into the manuscript the lack of progression of PERG compared to week 1' and acknowledge how measurements may be affected by SO presence. The secondary analysis comparing to week 1 rather than baseline is noted as problematic.

result: Visual acuity in SOHU eyes decreased rapidly at 1 week post-injection, with further progressive decreases at 5 and 8 weeks compared to 1 week, indicating progressive visual function deficits.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 questions whether 'OKR and PERG are reliable functional assessments if visual acuity is impaired due to difference in refractive index of SO' and asks whether baseline measurements were made before any intervention. Reviewer 1 notes 'if there was no progression for OKR and PERG, then it suggests that the SO bubble itself is the cause for the decreased amplitudes.' The editors request acknowledgment of how SO presence may affect measurements and note the lack of time 0 measurements.

result: The P1-N2 amplitude ratio of PERG in SO eyes to control eyes decreased significantly, consistent with visual acuity deficits.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 questions the reliability of PERG measurements given potential optical interference from SO and whether proper baseline controls were used. The editors specifically request that the manuscript acknowledge 'how PERG amplitude reduction may be due to the presence of the SO itself or limitations of detection by PERG.' The lack of progression compared to week 1 is noted as problematic.

result: RGC counts in peripheral retina showed no significant difference at 1 week post-injection, but significant progressive loss at 3, 5, and 8 weeks with only 43%, 28%, and 12% survival respectively.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 notes major inconsistency: 'In Figure 3, injection of SO ended up with 12% RGC survival by 8 weeks, while in Figure 4, counts of survival RGCs were ~60% by 8 weeks,' suggesting either 'a large neuroprotective effect by control AAV injection...or inconsistent neural damage from time to time in the SOHU model.' Reviewer 3 states 'such massive RGC death is only seen in severe crush or transection injury' and requests demonstration that this is not an ischemia-reperfusion experiment. Reviewer 1 questions the sampling methodology for peripheral vs. central retina.

result: Significant RGC axon degeneration occurred in SOHU optic nerves with only 57%, 41%, and 35% axon survival at 3, 5, and 8 weeks post-injection.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'the rate of RGC loss in this model is excessive' and notes it 'represents a very severe damage, similar to the situation of complete transection of the optic nerve, and it does not replicate the most cases of glaucoma.' Reviewer 3 requests demonstration that 'blood flow to the inner retina was not affected at early time points' and histology showing 'axonal transport block at and just behind the ONH' to prove the model mimics glaucoma rather than ischemia.

result: Control experiments show that SO intravitreal injection and small SO droplets with unstable IOP elevation do not cause significant neurodegeneration, indicating that the observed phenotypes are glaucomatous responses to ocular hypertension rather than SO toxicity.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these control experiments as demonstrating that neurodegeneration is IOP-dependent rather than due to SO toxicity. Reviewer 1 acknowledges the model 'differs from other established models' in having 'minimal tissue damage and inflammation.' No reviewer challenges the validity of these specific control experiments, though they question other aspects of the model.

result: Flushing SO from the anterior chamber quickly and stably lowered IOP back to normal, demonstrating that SOHU is a reversible model that can be used to test IOP-lowering effects on RGC degeneration.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the reversibility as a potential advantage. Reviewer 3 states 'removal of the oil to lower IOP is potentially useful adjunct, if one wishes to study various periods of IOP elevation, then allow time for further events at normal IOP.' No reviewer challenges the reversibility data itself, though they question other aspects of the model's mechanism and severity.

result: Extended pupillary dilation eventually allows IOP decline and SO removal quickly returns IOP to normal, providing evidence that trabecular meshwork function is normal in the SOHU model.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 questions the interpretation, stating the mechanism is 'almost surely not what is illustrated' and suggesting direct TM blockade by oil. Reviewer 1 asks 'how does the effect of IOP elevation in the posterior chamber differ from the anterior chamber?' and notes difficulty understanding the model. Reviewer 3 also notes the contradiction that 'waiting 15 minutes is not only completely impractical' but questions why this 'totally artificial, pupil-affected anesthetic state' would be representative of awake IOP.

result: IOP elevation in SOHU eyes produces progressive glaucomatous RGC and optic nerve degeneration starting at 3 weeks that correlates with visual function deficits and closely resembles changes in glaucoma patients, suggesting RGCs are sensitive to IOP elevation but resilient for a period before further degeneration.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 states the damage 'does not replicate the most cases of glaucoma' due to excessive severity. Reviewer 1 questions whether the model truly represents 'secondary pupillary block angle-closure glaucoma' and its implications for 'primary open angle glaucoma,' requesting 'a clearer discussion of how this model differs from human glaucoma and POAG.' Reviewer 3 requests demonstration that this is not 'more an ischemia-reperfusion experiment' and notes 'no histology is shown that the effect mimics OAG by having axonal transport block at and just behind the ONH.'

result: The SOHU model generates stable, robust IOP elevation and significant neurodegeneration within weeks, replicates secondary post-operative glaucoma and has features of acute secondary glaucoma, though it is not suitable for trabecular meshwork studies and its relevance to chronic primary glaucoma needs investigation.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 notes 'this type of postoperative secondary glaucoma is rare since surgeons prophylactically create peripheral iridotomies' and that 'secondary glaucoma caused by SO is more frequently the result of emulsification.' Reviewer 2 questions whether the model 'replicate[s] the most cases of glaucoma' given the excessive damage rate. Reviewer 3 states the model 'may make it harder for any protectant to block cell death with such severe and rapid damage' and notes 'every model in mice shows corneal enlargement...in the range reported here, so further studies of clarity need to be presented.'

result: After pupillary sealing by SO, the mouse lens with iris and ciliary body forms a rigid barrier disconnecting anterior and posterior chambers, causing IOP elevation in the posterior part but not the anterior chamber.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 directly challenges this mechanism, stating it is 'silly to assume that the iris is going to bow forward with an anterior chamber full of oil (2 microliters of oil is more than the normal anterior chamber volume).' Reviewer 2 notes 'TanoLab measures the pressure of the anterior chamber, thus is incapable of assessing the actual IOP value in the posterior part of the eye.' The editors request manometric readings to prove this compartmentalization.

result: The SOHU model leaves anterior segments unaffected with clear ocular elements allowing reliable in vivo assessment, while high posterior chamber IOP causes pronounced neurodegeneration within 5-8 weeks facilitating neuroprotectant testing.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 states 'every model in mice shows corneal enlargement (and axial length increase) with IOP in the range reported here, so further studies of clarity need to be presented.' Reviewer 1 questions whether visual function assessments are reliable given SO's different refractive index. Reviewer 3 notes the severe damage 'may make it harder for any protectant to block cell death with such severe and rapid damage,' questioning the utility for neuroprotectant screening.

result: Background claims about glaucoma pathophysiology: characterized by RGC axon injury and progressive degeneration, IOP level is the most common risk factor, and current therapies target IOP reduction.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 provides detailed corrections: the definition is 'incorrect and inexact' and should specify 'injury to the axons of RGC at the optic nerve head' with characteristic connective tissue changes. Reviewer 3 corrects that 'the risk factor is the level of the IOP, not elevated IOP' since 'half or more of those with open angle glaucoma...do not have "elevated" IOP.' Reviewer 3 also corrects that therapy aims to 'lower it sufficiently from baseline...to reduce progressive worsening' not to 'normalize' IOP.

result: Comparison to microbead model: produces excellent IOP elevation and neurodegeneration but has difficulties with bead retention, controlling outflow blockade, low success rate, high variability, lengthy duration, and limited RGC loss leaving narrow window for testing.
evaluation: Reviewer 3 directly refutes the success rate claim: 'Published data show that 95% of microbead injected mouse eyes achieve significant IOP elevation (Cone et al). This is not a "low success rate" and is actually better than the 80% rate reported here for their oil injections.' Reviewer 3 also notes 'the variability in rates of RGC loss is more typical for human OAG eyes, and no model of glaucoma can expect to have the same damage rate in every rodent eye.'
